book.title: Spell Freedom: The Underground Schools That Built the Civil Rights Movement
book.summary: The acclaimed author of the “stirring, definitive, and engrossing” (NPR) The Woman’s Hour returns with the story of four activists whose audacious plan to restore voting rights to Black Americans laid the groundwork for the Civil Rights Movement. In the summer of 1954, educator Septima Clark and small businessman Esau Jenkins travelled to rural Tennessee’s Highlander Folk School, an interracial training center for social change founded by Myles Horton, a white southerner with roots in the labor movement. There, the trio united behind a shared mission: preparing Black southerners to pass the daunting Jim Crow era voter registration literacy tests that were designed to disenfranchise them.

evidence: trade publisher signal: Simon & Schuster / Simon & Schuster

argument.statement: Underground voter-literacy schools helped restore Black voting rights and laid the groundwork for the Civil Rights Movement.

book.rationale: The book focuses on the actions of activists restoring voting rights for Black Americans during the Civil Rights Movement, making Race & Ethnicity the primary subject, with relevant connections to American History and Politics & Government.
